questions.q: What is the primary source for analyzing Kabir's character in this chapter—the biographical note, the poem, or both? Explain in one sentence.
questions.a: Both the biographical note and the poem are primary sources; the note gives historical context (weaver, disciple of Ramananda, iconoclast) while the poem reveals his inner voice, tone, and spiritual stance. A wrong answer that picks only one source shows the student hasn't grasped that character analysis in poetry requires synthesizing external facts with the speaker's own words.

questions.q: In the line "esjs rks fxjèkj xksiky] nwljks u dksbZ tk osQ flj eksj&eqoqQV", what does the phrase "eksj&eqoqQV" suggest about Kabir's attitude toward conventional worship? Answer in your own words.
questions.a: "eksj&eqoqQV" (bell and conch) symbolize ritualistic Hindu worship; Kabir's rejection ("nwljks u dksbZ tk osQ flj") shows he dismisses external rituals as irrelevant to true devotion. A wrong answer that merely translates the words without interpreting the symbolic rejection indicates the student is stuck at literal comprehension and misses the character trait of iconoclasm.

questions.q: Using the PEEL structure, write a four-sentence paragraph showing how the poem's opening line establishes Kabir's relationship with the divine. Use the line "esjs rks fxjèkj xksiky" as evidence.
questions.a: Point: Kabir addresses God as a personal, accessible master. Evidence: "esjs rks fxjèkj xksiky" (my lord is the king of Kashi). Explanation: By calling God "my king of Kashi" he claims an intimate, exclusive bond that bypasses priests and temples. Link: This possessive "esjs" (my) reflects his lifelong assertion of direct access to the divine. A weak answer that omits the "Link" step or fails to connect "esjs" to his biography shows inability to integrate text and context.

questions.q: Compare the Kabir of the biographical note (weaver, social reformer) with the Kabir speaking in the poem (devotee, rebel). What single character trait unifies both portrayals? Justify with one detail from each source.
questions.a: Fearless independence unifies both: the note says he "ges'kk fojksèk fd;k" (broke social and religious shackles) and the poem shows him rejecting ritual symbols ("nwljks u dksbZ tk osQ flj eksj&eqoqQV"). A wrong answer that lists two different traits (e.g., "humble" and "devout") misses the synthesis required at the analysis level.

questions.q: Critique this student statement: "Kabir's character is simply that of a devotee who loves God." Is it sufficient for a Class 11 answer? Why or why not?
questions.a: Insufficient. It ignores his rebellious tone, rejection of rituals, and the socio-historical context of a low-caste weaver challenging orthodoxy. A Class 11 answer must address complexity: Kabir is simultaneously a devotee, a social critic, and a poet who uses vernacular to democratize spirituality. A wrong answer that calls it "good enough" reveals the student equates character analysis with a single adjective.

questions.q: Compose a two-line doha in Hindi (or English) that captures Kabir's character as you understand it from this chapter, using the same rhyme scheme (AABB) as Kabir's dohas.
questions.a: Example: "जुलाहा तन साधु मन, जाति न पूछो कोय / अंतर राम बसे रे, खोलो अपना द्वार।" A good answer mirrors Kabir's vernacular style, contrasts social identity with spiritual essence, and uses the doha meter. A poor answer that writes a generic moral lesson without the tension of identity shows the student hasn't internalized Kabir's unique voice.
